terms.definition: writing programs that learn how to do a task from examples in data, instead of a person writing every rule.
what training produces: a rule, often a formula, that takes an input (such as a country's GDP per capita) and outputs an answer (such as a life-satisfaction score).
let the computer study examples whose answers are known and adjust the model until its answers come close to them.
a recipe a computer follows. A learning algorithm is the method that builds a model from data.
the model's answer for one input, e.g. a guessed life-satisfaction score for one country.
examples kept back from training and used once, at the very end, to check the finished model on data it never saw.
look at the data (tables, charts) to understand it before changing anything.
measure how good or bad a model's answers are, as a number.

two meanings in this book. (1) On the map: try other settings for the model and keep the ones that score best. (2) In lesson b05: train an already-trained model a little more on the task you really care about.
put the finished model into real use, so other systems or people get its answers.
the examples a model learns from.
one example, one row of the data: one email, or one country.
unwanted bulk email. Its opposite, a normal wanted email, is called ham.
the number you judge a program by, such as the share of emails it classifies correctly.
the share of answers that are right, e.g. 95 out of 100 emails classified correctly = 95% accuracy.
the share of answers that are wrong.
the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its number of people: roughly the average income per person, here in US dollars.
a country's average answer, on a scale from 0 to 10, to a survey question about how satisfied people are with their lives (the book takes it from the OECD Better Life Index).
digging through large amounts of data to find patterns nobody knew were there.
two columns are correlated when they tend to move together: when one goes up, the other tends to go up (or down) too.
random variation in the data that follows no pattern, so no model can predict it.
the known correct answer stored with an example, e.g. "spam", or a country's life-satisfaction score.
learning from examples that come with their labels.
predicting a class: one answer out of a fixed list, such as spam or not spam.
one of the fixed answers a classification model chooses between, e.g. spam or ham. (Python code also has classes; lesson b08 explains that second meaning where it appears.)
predicting a number, such as a car's price or a country's score.
another name for the label; the book uses it more when the answer is a number.
an input column the model uses, such as a car's mileage or a country's GDP per capita. Also called an attribute or a predictor.
another name for a feature: an input column.
another name for a feature: an input column. (A spam filter's "best predictors" are the words that tell spam apart best.)
a model used for classification, despite its name: it outputs the probability that an example belongs to a class.
the line where a classification model's answer changes from one class to the other: points on one side get one class, points on the other side get the other.
how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain); a 20% chance is a probability of 0.2.
learning from examples that have no labels, so the algorithm must find structure on its own.
grouping similar examples together, without being told what the groups are.
here: an algorithm that squeezes many columns into a 2D or 3D picture you can plot, keeping similar examples close together.
simplifying the data by using fewer columns while losing as little information as possible.
roughly, one column of the data. 2D means two dimensions: rows and columns, or the two axes of a flat picture.
making one new column out of several correlated ones, e.g. "wear and tear" out of a car's mileage and age.
the name of one particular visualization algorithm (Chapter 8).
flagging examples that are very different from the usual ones, after learning what "usual" looks like.
flagging examples of a kind never seen in training; it needs a training set with none of that kind in it.
an example far away from all the others.
finding which attributes tend to occur together, e.g. which products end up in the same basket.
learning from data where only a small part has labels and the rest has none.
learning from data with no labels by making labels out of the data itself, e.g. hiding part of each example and learning to fill it back in.
learning by trial and error: an agent acts, gets rewards or penalties, and learns which actions pay off.
in reinforcement learning, the learning system: it observes, acts, and gets rewards.
in reinforcement learning, a score for an action; a penalty is a negative reward.
in reinforcement learning, the world the agent acts in. ("Fluctuating environments" in lesson b02 just means situations that keep changing.)
in reinforcement learning, the agent's learned rule for which action to take in each situation.
reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for another task.
here: what a model has learned to notice about its inputs, e.g. what cat faces generally look like.
training once on all the data available, then using the model without it learning any more.
learning in small steps from new data as it arrives, while the model is in use. "Online" here means incremental, not "on the internet".
done separately from the live system, e.g. on a schedule, not while users are being served.
a small group of examples used for one learning step.
training on data too big for the computer's memory by loading one part at a time.
how big each learning step is: how quickly an online model adapts to new data (and forgets old data).
a model getting worse over time because the world changes and the model does not. Also called data drift.
the live system real users depend on, as opposed to your experiments.
do well on examples the model never saw during training.
learning by remembering the training examples and answering a new case from the most similar ones.
learning by fitting a model (e.g. a line) to the examples and answering new cases with the model.
a measure of how alike two examples are, e.g. the number of words two emails share, or how close two countries' GDP is.
an instance-based algorithm: find the k training examples most similar to the new case and average their answers.
a model whose answer is a starting value plus a fixed multiple of each input. With one input it is a straight line.
a number inside the model that training fills in, e.g. the two numbers that fix a straight line.
θ ("theta") is the Greek letter the book uses for model parameters: θ₀ is the line's starting value, θ₁ its slope.
how much a line rises for each step to the right; here, how much the score goes up per extra dollar of GDP.
where a line starts: its value when the input is 0. The book's θ₀.
a number that says how badly a model fits the training data; training pushes it down.
a number that says how well a model fits; training pushes it up.
train. `model.fit(X, y)` is the training call, and a model that fits the data well has small misses on it.
using a trained model to get answers for new cases.
the Python library for machine learning this book uses.
a Python library for tables (rows and named columns).
a table in pandas: rows plus named columns.
a Python library for fast grids of numbers (arrays).
a grid of numbers with no column names, as NumPy stores them.
a Python library for drawing charts.
a plain text file holding a table: one row per line, values separated by commas.
a chart with one dot per row, placed by two columns (one across, one up).
an ordered list of numbers, e.g. the 27 life-satisfaction scores.
a sample that is unrepresentative by chance, because it is too small.
a sample that is unrepresentative because of the way it was picked; making it bigger does not help.
two meanings. (1) One example, one row, as in the card of lesson b03: "one sample or all samples". (2) A set of rows picked from a bigger population, e.g. 27 of the world's countries.
a sample is representative when it looks like all the cases the model will meet later.
choosing, combining and creating the input columns a model gets.
the model fits the training data very well but does badly on new data, because it learned the noise too.
the model is too simple to learn the pattern, so it does badly even on the training data.
holding a model back (e.g. keeping its slope small) so it cannot follow the noise.
a setting of the learning algorithm that YOU choose before training, e.g. k in k-nearest neighbours; training does not change it.
how many independent numbers training may adjust; a line has two (its start and its slope).
a formula with the input raised to powers (x, x², x³, ...). Degree 10 goes up to x¹⁰, so the curve can bend many times.
root mean squared error: square every miss, average them, take the square root. A typical size of miss, in the same units as the answer.
how wrong the model is on new cases; the test set gives an estimate of it.
examples held back from the training set to compare candidate models, before the test set is ever used.
kept aside and not used for learning.
comparing models many times over on several small validation sets, then averaging, instead of trusting one split.
the training data does not look like the data the model will meet in production.
examples held out from the training data (not from the production-like data), used to tell overfitting apart from data mismatch.
a result saying that, with no assumptions about the data, no model is better than any other in advance.
a model that answers by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the inputs (Chapter 6).
a common clustering algorithm: it looks for k groups and a centre for each (Chapter 9).
a grid of numbers with rows and columns; `X` here is a matrix of 27 rows and 1 column.
the size of an array or table, written (rows, columns): (27, 1) is 27 rows and 1 column.
a single column in pandas: a list of values with no column name around it.
NumPy's usual type for numbers with decimals, e.g. 5.8.
the labels pandas gives the rows, 0, 1, 2 and so on; or, in general, a position in a list.
a document (Jupyter, Google Colab) where code cells and their output sit together.
a Python file of ready-made code that you load with `import`, e.g. `matplotlib.pyplot`.
in Python, one thing held in a variable, carrying its own stored values and functions; `model` is an object.
the middle value once a list is sorted.
the language for querying database tables (`SELECT`, `WHERE`, `CASE WHEN`); the lessons use it for comparisons.
